question:
(a) Establish that $\sec^{-1}x=\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)$ for $|x|\geq1$ and $\csc^{-1}x=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)$ for $|x|\geq1$.

(b) Hence evaluate $\sec^{-1}(-2)+\csc^{-1}(-2)$ using principal values.
explanation:
(a)
Let
$$\theta=\sec^{-1}x$$
Then $\sec\theta=x$, where $|x|\geq1$. Therefore,
$$\cos\theta=\frac{1}{x}$$
The principal-value range of $\sec^{-1}$ agrees with the range of $\cos^{-1}$ after excluding $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. Hence,
$$\theta=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$$
Thus,
$$\sec^{-1}x=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$$
Similarly, let
$$\phi=\csc^{-1}x$$
Then $\csc\phi=x$, so
$$\sin\phi=\frac{1}{x}$$
The principal-value ranges of $\csc^{-1}$ and $\sin^{-1}$ agree for the permitted non-zero values. Therefore,
$$\csc^{-1}x=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$$

(b)
Using the established relations,
$$\sec^{-1}(-2)=\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{2\pi}{3}$$
and
$$\csc^{-1}(-2)=\sin^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\frac{\pi}{6}$$
Therefore,
$$\sec^{-1}(-2)+\csc^{-1}(-2)=\frac{2\pi}{3}-\frac{\pi}{6}$$
$$=\frac{4\pi-\pi}{6}=\frac{\pi}{2}$$
Hence, the required value is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
